activities.caption: generative or evaluative? file each method
activities.name: uxrGenEvalSort

config.prompt: Two grand divisions — file each method where it belongs:

items.label: interviews digging beneath a feature request
five participants on real tasks in a draft
a diary study of low-frequency routines
an A/B test between two checkout variants
contextual inquiry at the actual workplace
severity-rated findings from a usability session

config.why: Generative work identifies and defines what hurts; evaluative work puts a draft in front of people and watches what breaks. Naming which half a study serves is the first habit of a plan.

activities.caption: pair each question with its instrument
activities.name: uxrQuestionMatch

config.prompt: Method follows question — pair each with its fitting instrument:

pairs.left: a why question — where does the current world hurt?
a how-well question — can they complete the task?
a how-many question — which variant moves the rate?
a once-a-year behaviour nobody can schedule

config.why: Each instrument answers a different shape of question — choosing the method for the fashion rather than the question is how a study drifts off-target.

activities.caption: sequence one round of usability testing
activities.name: uxrSessionOrder

config.prompt: One round of the loop, in the order the craft runs it:
items: Recruit five participants who resemble the actual audience
Hand over a task, not an instruction: 'pay this invoice'
Stay silent while the participant thinks aloud
Watch the hesitation, wrong menus and backtracking
Rate findings by severity, then fix the criticals
Run five participants again on the revised design
config.why: The loop, not the number, is the method: small, fast, iterative beats large, slow, single-shot — each round reveals what the previous redesign exposed.

config.prompt: The System Usability Scale is scored out of 100. Decades of benchmarked data put the industry average at roughly what?
config.why: ~68 — the reason the instrument means something is that its distribution is public: 80+ reads as strong, and a bespoke satisfaction score has no such history until you build one.
config.context: Benchmark against known baselines, never against nothing.

activities.caption: plan a field study — pick the path
activities.name: uxrFieldBranch

config.root: A study of nurses using a new rota tool is being planned. Walk the decisions.

start.text: How do you observe the shift?

choices.label: Sit in the nurses' station through the handover
choices.feedback: In-context visits catch what the lab never sees — the workaround taped to the monitor exists only to be visited.

choices.label: Invite the nurses to the office lab and have them replay the shift
choices.feedback: The lab strips the context that causes the behaviour — the shadow systems never show up in a meeting room.

consent.text: The ward manager offers: 'Skip the consent forms, everyone is busy.'

choices.label: No — informed consent first: what is recorded, how data is used, the right to stop
choices.feedback: Ethics is not paperwork — consent, privacy of recordings and care with vulnerable participants are how the values survive scale.

choices.label: Fine, verbal permission is enough
choices.feedback: Recordings made without informed consent break the profession's conscience — and the trust the next study depends on.

labterm.text: Context does the causing: what people do when nobody from the study is watching is exactly what the visit is for.

done.text: Consented, observed in place, synthesised systematically — the unglamorous half done first is what makes the findings valid.

verbal.text: The study now has data it cannot ethically use — research operations (consent flows, secure repositories) exist precisely to prevent this.

config.why: Recruiting and ethics decide validity before the first participant — no analysis rescues a study that watched the wrong people the wrong way.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — in-context methods
activities.name: uxrContextSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about in-context methods is backwards — click it:
lines: Contextual inquiry watches people work in their own environment.
The master-apprentice stance: watch first, ask in the moment, interpret together.
Diary studies capture low-frequency events — the monthly payday routine, the annual tax scramble.
Field notes and diary entries are fine as raw anecdotes — no systematic synthesis needed.
Both methods ask what the context does to the behaviour.
config.correction: The weight is the cost: notes and entries need affinity mapping and timeline reconstruction, or they stay anecdotes instead of becoming findings.
config.why: Analysis weight is why these methods pair with the defining stage's synthesis discipline rather than replacing the fast five-user loop.

activities.caption: behavioural vs attitudinal metrics — drag the divider
activities.name: uxrMetricsCompare

config.prompt: The two halves of the metric taxonomy — drag between them:

before.label: Behavioural — what they did
before.text: Task success rate, time on task, error count and type — collected while the user works, they locate where the design confuses. Faster is not always better on exploration tasks.

after.label: Attitudinal — what they said
after.text: The System Usability Scale's ten fixed items, task-level confidence and easiness ratings — attested attitudes benchmarked against a public distribution (68 average, 80+ strong).

config.why: Engagement numbers reward addiction as readily as value, and no single number should carry a decision — the triangulation rule applies within metrics as much as across methods.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the reporting discipline
activities.name: uxrReportCloze

config.text: Rank findings by %%0%% × severity × impact on the decision, attach the %%1%% — clips, quotes, numbers — beneath each claim, and after launch %%2%% the decision so the function calibrates itself against reality.
config.hint: The first is how often the problem showed up; the last is the closure habit of the mature practice.
